world_behind.title: A city awake at night
world_behind.text: Laban has been "out by night among them" (v. 22) — the elders of the Jews, meeting after dark while Babylon's shadow lengthens. The record's Jerusalem is jittery, armed, and conferring late; a garrison commander drunk in the street after such a meeting fits the era's nerves exactly.

world_behind.title: The sword of an officer
world_behind.text: A hilt of "pure gold" (v. 9) and a blade of "the most precious steel" (v. 9) describe a commander's ceremonial weapon, the kind worn as rank. The blade outlived its owner by a thousand years: Nephi carried it to the new world, copied it for his people's defense, and the kings kept it as a royal relic (2 Ne. 5:14; Mosiah 1:16).

world_behind.title: Treasuries held words, not just wealth
world_behind.text: The records sit in Laban's treasury, under a keeper who carries "the keys of the treasury" (v. 20). Archives and valuables shared a room in the ancient world, and Zoram reads less like a valet than a trusted records-officer — which explains both his access and his easy talk of the elders' business.

world_behind.title: Oaths ended pursuit
world_behind.text: One sworn sentence from Zoram and "our fears did cease concerning him" (v. 37). In that world an oath was not a promise to try; it was binding speech before God, and both sides of this scene treat it as stronger than ropes. The family's security plan for its flight rests entirely on it.

cites.quote: our fears did cease concerning him

spans.text: our fears did cease concerning him

world_behind.title: Bloodguilt was the law's default
world_behind.text: Nephi's protest — "Never at any time have I shed the blood of man" (v. 10) — is the voice of a law that made shed blood the gravest of debts (Gen. 9:6). The scene's agony is legal and religious at once: only a direct divine warrant could override the default, and the record makes the warrant carry that exact weight.

cites.quote: Never at any time have I shed the blood of man

spans.text: Never at any time have I shed the blood of man

world_behind.title: David's night scene, remembered
world_behind.text: Israel's stories already held a sleeping enemy delivered into a young man's hand — and David twice refused the stroke his men urged (1 Sam. 24; 26). Lehi's family knew those stories. The chapter walks the same ground to a different ending, and the difference, a command given, is the whole matter.

words.text: The Spirit's verb is pressure, not invitation: to constrain is to press against resistance. The record uses it precisely — Nephi is "constrained by the Spirit" (v. 10) in the same verse that records his recoil. Revelation here is not a warm impression confirming what he wanted; it is a force meeting an honest, resisting conscience.

The body's vote: "I shrunk and would that I might not slay him" (v. 10). The record preserves Nephi's flinch on purpose. A narrator building a hero would have cut it; a witness keeping honest accounts kept it, and the flinch is what lets a reader trust everything else in the scene.

cites.quote: I shrunk and would that I might not slay him

spans.text: I shrunk and would that I might not slay him

words.text: The rationale's key verb, and a new one for the record: not destruction but slow fade: a nation dying by forgetting, generation by generation, "in unbelief" (v. 13). The word names the exact disease the plates exist to prevent, and the volume will keep the phrase as its standing diagnosis for peoples who lose the word.

"yea, even every whit" (v. 19). A whit is the smallest possible amount, an old idiom for totality. Nephi's disguise is complete down to the armor, and the little word carries the scene's strangeness: the shepherd of the record dressed entirely, exactly, as the man the Lord just judged.

phrases.text: Nephi's answer to fear is a recital: Moses spoke, "the waters of the Red Sea" (v. 2) divided, "our fathers came through, out of captivity, on dry ground" (v. 2). Borrowed history is his courage. The family is camped by that same sea's shore, which turns the old story from illustration into map.

cites.quote: the waters of the Red Sea

spans.text: the waters of the Red Sea

cites.quote: our fathers came through, out of captivity, on dry ground

spans.text: our fathers came through, out of captivity, on dry ground

phrases.term: led by the Spirit, not knowing beforehand
phrases.text: The chapter's method stated in one clause. Two planned attempts have failed; the successful one enters the city without a plan at all. The phrase becomes the record's standing description of how God moves his servants — walking first, seeing after — and Nephi writes it without embarrassment.

phrases.term: the workmanship thereof was exceedingly fine
phrases.text: A craftsman's formula, sounded here over a sword at the worst moment of Nephi's life — and he will use the same words later for the ship (1 Ne. 18:4) and his people's temple (2 Ne. 5:16). The eye that appraises fine work in gold and steel is the same eye that will build a civilization's tools; the record keeps the phrase as his signature.

The angel's promise (1 Ne. 3:29) returns as present fact, spoken three times in the scene (v. 11, 12, 17). Repetition is the point: the warrant is not Nephi's inference but a delivered word, insisted upon until he acts on it.

phrases.term: It is better that one man should perish
phrases.text: The hardest sentence in the chapter states a principle with a long shadow: one man weighed against a nation's faith. Caiaphas will reason in the same shape about Jesus (John 11:50); the words nearly rhyme, and the two scenes judge each other: the principle is only as good as the one who speaks it, which is why the record grounds it in the Lord's voice and not in Nephi's arithmetic.

phrases.term: as the Lord liveth, and as I live
phrases.text: The oath of 1 Nephi 3:15 returns, now offered to a stranger. Nephi binds himself before asking Zoram to be bound, and the exchange of oaths, his for Zoram's, turns captor and captive into companions within the same scene. The unit's oath economy runs on two sentences, and both hold.

verses.label: v. 1–3
verses.title: The fifty, answered
verses.text: Nephi replies to his brothers' arithmetic in kind: Laban "and his fifty" (v. 1), or "even than his tens of thousands" (v. 1), set against "mightier than all the earth" (v. 1). Then the recital: ye know it is true, ye know an angel spoke, "wherefore can ye doubt" (v. 3) The speech works — they follow — but the record notes they went "yet wroth" (v. 4), murmuring while walking. Obedience and belief are already coming apart in this family.

cites.quote: even than his tens of thousands

spans.text: even than his tens of thousands

verses.label: v. 5–6
verses.title: Into the city blind
verses.text: Alone, at night, Nephi walks toward the house of the man who robbed him, and the record gives the method: "I was led by the Spirit, not knowing beforehand the things which I should do" (v. 6). After a lot and a fortune have failed, the errand's actual key is a man willing to walk without seeing the next step.

cites.quote: I was led by the Spirit, not knowing beforehand the things which I should do

spans.text: I was led by the Spirit, not knowing beforehand the things which I should do

verses.label: v. 7–9
verses.title: A drunk man and a beautiful sword
verses.text: Providence arrives without drama: no battle, just a commander "fallen to the earth" (v. 7) in a stupor. What the record dwells on is the sword — gold, steel, fine work — a craftsman's paragraph in the middle of dread, and the blade that will hang over the whole civilization's history enters the story admired before it is used.

verses.label: v. 10–13
verses.title: The constraint and the recoil
verses.text: The scene the record slows for. The Spirit speaks three times; between the first word and the stroke stand Nephi's protest, his flinch, and a stack of reasons — delivered into thy hands, he sought thy life, he would not hearken, he took your property — capped by the principle of v. 13. The record holds the reader in the hesitation because that is where its honesty lives; the killing is presented as the costliest obedience in the book.

verses.label: v. 14–17
verses.title: Remembering decides
verses.text: What finally moves Nephi is none of the reasons but a memory: the covenant of 1 Nephi 2:20, quoted back word for word: "Inasmuch as thy seed shall keep my commandments, they shall prosper" (v. 14). No law, no keeping; no plates, no law (v. 15–16). The unborn outweigh the fallen man, and Nephi obeys as a man doing arithmetic about his descendants' souls.

cites.quote: Inasmuch as thy seed shall keep my commandments, they shall prosper

spans.text: Inasmuch as thy seed shall keep my commandments, they shall prosper

verses.label: v. 20–27
verses.title: In the dead man's clothes
verses.text: The disguise scenes run on dramatic irony: Zoram chattering about the elders to the man who has just executed his master, the voice imitation, the brothers fleeing from what they take to be Laban. Nephi walks out through the machinery of the city's elite wearing its uniform — the office Laban forfeited leaves the city on other shoulders, carrying the records it existed to keep.

verses.label: v. 31–38
verses.title: Oaths make a household
verses.text: Fear ends the chapter, and oaths end the fear: Nephi's sworn promise of freedom — "a free man like unto us" (v. 33) — answered by Zoram's sworn promise to stay. The family's first convert joins on words alone, and the company that left camp as four brothers returns with the plates and a fifth man.

cites.quote: a free man like unto us

spans.text: a free man like unto us

chapter.title: The chapter the record slows down for
chapter.text: The beheading takes one verse; the deciding takes eight. That ratio is the record's ethics in miniature: what matters is not the stroke but the warrant, and the narrative spends its time exactly where the moral weight sits.

chapter.title: Success by inversion
chapter.text: The two failed attempts were plans — protocol by lot, purchase by fortune. The successful attempt has no plan: one man, at night, "not knowing beforehand" (v. 6). The chapter completes the argument chapter 3 began about means: human competence got its turns first, so that no reader could mistake whose errand this was.

chapter.title: How the text holds the killing
chapter.text: It preserves the protest and the flinch; it stacks reasons rather than asserting one; it grounds the decisive principle in the Lord's voice, not Nephi's judgment; and it lets the final motive be covenant-memory about children not yet born. What it never does is enjoy the scene or apologize for it. The reader is given everything Nephi had, in the order he had it, and left where he was left — commanded.

chapter.title: A title deed, told honestly
chapter.text: Why tell this at all, decades later? Because the plates' provenance passes through this night, and the record documents its own chain of custody: promise (1 Ne. 3:29), delivery (v. 11–17), possession (v. 38). A cleaner story would have been easy to write. The record chooses instead to hold its founding object with unwashed hands, and its credibility elsewhere is bought here.

chapter.title: Nephi in Laban's shape
chapter.text: Garments, armor, sword, voice — for one night the younger brother wears the establishment whole, "even every whit" (v. 19). The image cuts two ways: judgment on an office abandoned to appetite, and a quiet warning the record will develop for the rest of its length — the sword of Laban stays in Nephite hands, and so does the temptation it stands for.

chapter.title: The records half of the unit closes
chapter.text: Verse 38 brings plates, servant, and brothers down to the tent: the departure unit's scripture errand is done. Chapter 5 will open the plates and read; chapter 7 will run the same road again for families. Records first, households second — the unit's order is its argument about what a colony cannot survive without.

chapter.title: Zoram, the first addition
chapter.text: The book's first conversion is not a sermon's fruit but an oath's: a records-keeper offered freedom, "did take courage" (v. 35), and bound himself to a fugitive family in the dark. The record treats his oath as fully equal to the brothers' blood ties — a founding precedent for a people that will be defined by covenant rather than descent.

applications.title: Recite your Red Seas
applications.text: Nephi's courage was borrowed from history he trusted. Build the personal recital: two or three past deliverances (family ones count) told well enough to say out loud when the next fifty appears. Courage that has a text beats courage that has a mood.

applications.title: Walk without the whole map
applications.text: The errand's turning point was a man willing to move while ignorant of step two. Identify the commanded thing you are postponing until the plan is complete, and take its first step this week on the strength of the instruction you already have.

applications.title: Let the recoil be part of obedience
applications.text: Nephi's shrinking was not weakness of faith; it was a working conscience meeting a hard command, and the record kept it. If this chapter itself troubles you, you are reading it the way its writer lived it. When duty collides with your recoil, keep both in the record — pray the hesitation honestly rather than performing an ease you do not feel.

applications.title: Decide from the covenant, not the moment
applications.text: What settled Nephi was remembered scripture aimed at his descendants. For your next hard decision, ask the question he asked: which choice serves the people downstream of me — and which promise of God bears on them?

applications.title: Notice whose clothes you are wearing
applications.text: Position, title, uniform: Laban had them all and served himself in them. Whatever office you hold, in family or church or work, name one way the office could become a costume, and one practice that keeps the person inside it honest.

applications.title: Offer the oath first
applications.text: Nephi bound himself before asking Zoram for anything. In a strained relationship, be the first to commit. State plainly what the other person can count on from you, and let your promise create the safety their promise needs.

questions.text: Whose "fifty" am I currently counting, and what past deliverance am I leaving out of the arithmetic?
When did I last act on a prompting without knowing beforehand, and what did I learn about being led that planning has never taught me?
What is my honest recoil right now, the thing conscience or comfort resists, and have I prayed it rather than only felt it?
Which commandments could my children not keep if I failed to hand them the words, and what am I doing about the handing?
Where in my life am I wearing a uniform that is doing the believing for me?
Whom do I resemble from the outside, and would the resemblance survive my voice being heard at length?
What oath-sized promise would give courage to someone currently trembling near me, and am I willing to swear it first?
